land.text: the Southern District of Gran Colombia that became the State of Ecuador on 13 May 1830

predecessors.note: Cliopatria draws Ecuador inside Gran Colombia to 1833; the Gran Colombia dossier removes it from 1830.

correction.text: modern Ecuador without the Galapagos until 12 February 1832, the State of Ecuador that left Gran Colombia on 13 May 1830

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1830-1833: Cliopatria's Ecuador row begins in 1834 but the infobox gives 'from Gran Colombia: 13 May 1830'; the Gran Colombia row of 1830-1833 still draws Ecuador inside Gran Colombia (marked wrong in that dossier). The outline is Cliopatria's 1834 shape (modern Ecuador with the Galapagos, which Ecuador 'formally occupied and claimed ... on 12 February 1832'); before that date the islands are nobody's. The Ecuador page says the Treaty of Pasto of 1832 turned the Department of Cauca over to New Granada but does not say when Ecuador took it; the Gran Colombia dossier draws Cauca in New Granada, so it is left out here.

262,830 km2 for 1834-1904 against the infobox's 283,561 km2 (276,841 km2 without the Galapagos): ratio 0.93, so the shape is modern Ecuador with the islands. Until the Rio Protocol of 29 January 1942 the frontier on the Peruvian side was the 1936 status quo line of 'de facto possession'; relative to it Ecuador ceded 18,552 km2 and received 5,072 km2 in 1942 (net 13,480 km2, 5 percent of the shape), and the pre-1942 line cannot be drawn from a page, so the shape stands. The claims north to the Caqueta and east to the Amazon given up in 1904 (Tobar-Rio Branco, 6 May 1904) and 1916 (Munoz-Suarez, 15 July 1916) are not in it. Unverified: page budget (no page gives the 1834-1904 frontier).

262,773 km2 for 1905-1949, 57 km2 below 1834 (a redraw). Covers the 1941 war, in which Peru occupied El Oro, Loja and Zamora Chinchipe (shape unchanged; the occupations are in the ledger) and the Rio Protocol of 29 January 1942 (Peru received about 200,000 km2 of disputed Maynas territory, which was claimed but not in the shape).
262,658 km2 for 1950-1952: one cell of Peru's Tumbes missing against 1905 and 1953, a one-cell artifact; no page opened dates a change in 1950.

262,773 km2 for 1953-2023, identical to 1905. The pages date no change after 1942 except the demarcation: the Brasilia Presidential Act of 26 October 1998 settled the dispute and formal demarcation began on 13 May 1999; about 78 km stayed unmarked from 1948 to 1998.
Identical to 1953-2023 (262,773 km2; ratio 0.93 to the infobox's 283,561 km2).

region.text: the Southern District of Gran Colombia as the State of Ecuador, without the Galapagos

ledger.note: 13 May 1830: Ecuador leaves Gran Colombia. Infobox 'from Gran Colombia: 13 May 1830'; 'the Gran Colombia ceased to exist when it divided itself into three different nations'. The page names no boundary, so the region is Cliopatria's 1834 outline.

12 February 1832: Ecuador claims the Galapagos Islands. They 'formally occupied and claimed the islands on 12 February 1832'; the Ecuador page says 'Two years later, it annexed the Galapagos Islands'. The islands were unclaimed before.

1859: Peru occupies and blockades Guayaquil. The dispute followed Ecuador's agreement (1857-1860) to give British creditors land in the Canelos region, which Peru objected to; President Castilla occupied and blockaded Guayaquil in 1859 (the Ecuador page says Peru 'briefly occupied Guayaquil again in 1860'). The page gives no month.

25 February 1860: the Treaty of Mapasingue ends the crisis. 'Ecuador voided the concession of territories claimed by Peru to the British'; the page says the treaty ended the crisis and does not date the withdrawal from Guayaquil.

23 July 1941: Peru invades the coast. 'The Peruvian offensive against Ecuador began on July 23' and on 31 July, before the ceasefire took effect, Peruvian paratroopers took Puerto Bolivar; 'By the end of August 1941, Peru occupied the coast: the provinces and cantons of El Oro, Puerto Bolivar...'.

August 1941: Peru holds the southern mountains. 'In the mountains, the provinces and cantons of Loja and Zamora Chinchipe were occupied'; the page gives no date inside 1941 for it (by the end of August is the coast's).
1942: Peru leaves Loja and Zamora Chinchipe. The page gives no date for these provinces; the year follows the Rio Protocol and the Peru dossier.
12 February 1942: Peru leaves El Oro. The Rio Protocol was signed on 29 January 1942 and 'on February 12, 1942, Peruvian troops vacated the Ecuadorian province of El Oro'.

wars.name: Ecuadorian-Peruvian War of 1859-1860 (Guayaquil blockade)
wars.outcome: Peru occupied and blockaded Guayaquil in 1859 over Ecuador's cession of Canelos land to British creditors; the Treaty of Mapasingue (25 February 1860) ended the crisis and Ecuador voided the concession.
wars.note: The page does not call this a war; it is listed because it moved no border but held Ecuador's main port.

wars.name: Ecuadorian-Peruvian War
wars.outcome: Peru occupied El Oro, Loja and Zamora Chinchipe between 23 July and the end of August 1941; the ceasefire took effect on 31 July 1941, the Talara Accord followed on 2 October and the Rio Protocol on 29 January 1942, after which Peru left El Oro (12 February 1942).
wars.note: First shots 5 July 1941 (the sides disagree on who fired first). Relative to the 1936 status quo line Ecuador ceded 18,552 km2 and Peru ceded 5,072 km2 (Ecuadorian-Peruvian territorial dispute page); Peru received about 200,000 km2 of disputed Maynas territory. Ecuador declared the Protocol null on 29 September 1960.

wars.name: Paquisha War
wars.outcome: A January-February 1981 clash over three watchposts in the disputed Cordillera del Condor; no border changed.
wars.note: Dated only as January-February 1981 on the dispute page.

wars.name: Cenepa War
wars.outcome: Fought 26 January - 28 February 1995; the Brasilia Presidential Act of 26 October 1998 settled the dispute and formal demarcation began on 13 May 1999.
wars.note: The dispute page names no zone for the fighting, so none is given.

certainty.note: The Amazonian frontier was claimed, not held (Maynas); the Brazilian line is treaty-fixed from 6 May 1904 and the Colombian from 15 July 1916; the 1936 status quo line was 'de facto possession'.
The Rio Protocol of 29 January 1942 set a 'definitive border line'; about 78 km stayed unmarked and Ecuador declared the Protocol null on 29 September 1960.
Demarcation began on 13 May 1999 after the Brasilia Presidential Act of 26 October 1998.

notes:
Four pages opened (the budget is five): the Ecuador article, the Ecuadorian-Peruvian territorial dispute page, the Ecuadorian-Peruvian War page and the Galapagos Islands page.

Cliopatria's Ecuador is modern Ecuador (262,830 km2, ratio 0.93 to the infobox's 283,561 km2) for every year, so there is nothing to correct in the shapes except the missing 1830-1833 years (new keyframe). The real story is what the shape does not hold: the Amazonian claim to Maynas (about 200,000 km2 passed to Peru in 1942, 18,552 km2 of it against the 1936 line), the claims north to the Caqueta given up in 1916 and the claims between the Caqueta and the Amazon given up to Brazil in 1904 (Tobar-Rio Branco, 6 May 1904). They are in the wars, the keyframe notes and this file, not in the ledger, because they changed no drawn cell. Peru's side of the 1941 events is in the Peru dossier (occupations mirrored; no 1859-1860 event there).
Not settled: when Ecuador took the Department of Cauca and Pasto (the page says only that the Treaty of Pasto of 1832 'turned over' Cauca to New Granada); the Loja and Zamora Chinchipe withdrawal date; the Paquisha and Cenepa zones; the Pedemonte-Mosquera Protocol (11 August 1830, which Peru denies exists); the Pando-Noboa Treaty (12 July 1832), where Peru recognised Ecuador; 10 February 1832, when Colombia recognised its separation (dispute page); the 1859-1860 occupation month; the Loja Federal State (not on the Ecuador page). Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas passed to Peru under the 1829 armistice (Gran Colombia dossier).
